audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Psychology bachelor combines the study of behaviour and the brain with research methods and professional skills.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The 2026–2027 example follows the Brain, Cognition and Behaviour specialisation. Maastricht awards credits by study year. The table breaks each year down by the published workload. UCR offers three related ways to study psychology.

curriculum.routeLabel: Brain, Cognition and Behaviour specialisation (year 3, 24 EC)

cellNotes.text: Both introduce biological and social perspectives on behaviour. UCR emphasises brain and behaviour. Maastricht brings in a wider range of psychological perspectives.
Both study social cognition and group behaviour. Maastricht also examines personality and individual differences.
Both study cognitive, emotional and social development across the lifespan.
Both connect the brain to behaviour. UCR uses comparative neurobiology and laboratory methods. Maastricht also studies imaging and brain stimulation.
Both study memory and attention with experimental approaches. Maastricht also examines perception as prediction.
Both study how the brain guides action. UCR focuses on perception and motor control. Maastricht also studies motivation.
Maastricht offers a dedicated cognitive neuroscience methods module. UCR uses related methods within perception and cognition courses.
Both examine how drugs act. UCR covers pharmacology across body systems. Maastricht focuses on the biology of behaviour and psychoactive drugs.
Both examine questions about the mind. UCR focuses on philosophy of mind. Maastricht also studies computational models of cognition.
Both study psychological assessment and its ethical implications. UCR adds psychotherapy approaches. Maastricht also develops psychometric analysis.
Both examine biases, fallacies and the evaluation of claims. UCR focuses on misinformation and scientific credibility.
Both introduce research methods and statistics. UCR includes research design, surveys and analysis of variance.
Both study statistical models for experimental data. UCR uses regression, variance analysis and related methods.
Both develop programming in Python. UCR also covers object-oriented programming. Maastricht applies programming to examples from psychology.
Maastricht uses a supervised small-group project covering the empirical research cycle. UCR’s optional independent research sits outside the scheduled courses.
Both apply psychological research to societal problems. UCR focuses on youth radicalisation and resilience. Maastricht covers a broader range of problems and perspectives.
UCR develops academic writing, research literacy and civic engagement. Maastricht includes a programme of psychology-specific professional skills and portfolio work.
Maastricht develops psychology-specific professional communication and reflective practice.
Maastricht includes a third year of professional and life skills alongside a competency portfolio.
Maastricht students choose 24 EC of electives. Options include faculty courses or an approved external package.

notes.text: Maastricht includes dedicated cognitive neuroscience methods, psychology-specific professional skills, a supervised empirical project and a 24 EC specialisation. UCR covers related subjects across psychology, brain and behaviour, statistics and neighbouring disciplines.

Maastricht assesses each 60 EC year as a study unit through a portfolio and competency exam. The programme overview mentions a Year 3 thesis, and the regulations list no separate thesis credit allocation. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled coursework.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.text: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.text: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

BENENTR211.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
BENENTR211.text: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.

BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.text: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

DISARIN111.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
